faqs.a: SVG is a vector format that scales perfectly, but many platforms — social media, document editors, printers — only accept raster images like PNG. Converting an SVG to PNG at the right pixel size prepares it for those platforms.
The tool reads the width, height or viewBox of your file. If none are present it reports an error, because the browser cannot rasterize a dimension-less SVG.
faqs.q: How does the tool know the SVG size?

faqs.a: With the lock on, changing the width recalculates the height to keep the same proportions, and vice versa. Turn it off only if you intentionally want to stretch the graphic.

faqs.a: Larger PNGs are sharper on high-density screens but take more memory and disk space. For web use, 1024–2048 px on the long edge is usually plenty; for print, aim for your target size in inches times 300.

keyFacts: SVG files store vector shapes; PNG files store a fixed grid of pixels.
Browsers rasterize SVG by drawing it into an image element on a canvas.
An SVG needs real dimensions (width/height or viewBox) to be rasterized.
The aspect-ratio lock preserves proportions: height = width × (sourceH ÷ sourceW).
PNG keeps transparency; optional white or black backgrounds flatten it.
All conversion happens locally with the canvas API.

svg-to-png-converter.quickAnswer: This tool converts SVG files to PNG at the exact size you choose. Upload an .svg file, type the target width and height (the aspect-ratio lock keeps proportions correct), pick a background, and download the PNG. The pixel-count readout tells you exactly how large the result is.
svg-to-png-converter.workedExample:
You upload an SVG logo that is 300 × 200 px and keep the aspect lock on.

You type target width = 1200.
Locked height = 1200 × (200 ÷ 300) = 1200 × 0.6667 = 800 px.
Pixel count = 1200 × 800 = 960,000 pixels.

The PNG downloads as logo-1200x800.png — a 4× enlargement that stays perfectly sharp because the source was vector.
